title: Growth, Reproduction and Behavior
bigQuestion: How do living things get the energy to grow, sense their world, and make sure there is a next generation?

story.title: The Bee, the Flower and an Old Deal
story.kicker: A clover blossom and a honeybee are trading partners in a deal older than any human city.
paragraphs: It is a warm June morning in a vacant lot on the South Side of Chicago. White clover has taken over a patch of cracked ground. A honeybee lands on one blossom. She pushes her head into a tiny flower, uncurls a tongue like a straw, and drinks. What she is drinking is nectar, a sugar water the plant made from sunlight, air, and rain. She did not make that sugar. The plant did, and it is giving it away.

As the bee drinks, yellow dust sticks to the fuzz on her body. The dust is pollen. Each grain carries half of what it takes to make a new clover seed. The bee does not want the pollen. She wants the nectar. But she is covered in pollen anyway, and when she flies to the next blossom, some of it rubs off. That blossom now has what it needs to make seeds. The plant paid a little sugar and got its pollen delivered.

Back at the hive, the bee passes the nectar to other workers, who fan it with their wings until it thickens into honey. The colony will eat that honey all winter, when no flowers bloom. Some of the pollen goes into the hive too, as food for young bees. So the sugar the clover made from sunlight ends up powering thousands of bees through a Chicago January.

Neither the bee nor the clover planned any of this. Bees that were better at finding nectar left more offspring. Flowers that fed bees got more pollen delivered and made more seeds. Over millions of years the two shaped each other. The flower's color, its scent, and its shape are a sign that says: land here. The bee's fuzzy body and its ability to remember which flowers pay best are its side of the deal.

This chapter follows that flow. It starts with how a plant turns light into sugar and how a bee turns sugar into flight. It moves to how living things sense the world, remember it, and act. And it ends with the many ways living things make sure there is a next generation, from a bee's dance to a maple seed's spin.
story.think: The bee and the clover both benefit, but neither one is trying to help the other. What does each one actually want, and how does the deal still work?

sections.title: Matter and Energy in Living Things

lessons.title: Making Food From Light
lessons.mainIdea: Plants use light energy to combine carbon dioxide and water into sugar, releasing oxygen.
reading: A tiny acorn falls in a forest preserve in Cook County. Sixty years later it is an oak weighing many tons. Where did all that wood come from? Not from the soil. Almost all of it came from the air. That sounds impossible until you understand *photosynthesis*, the way plants make their own food.

Inside the chloroplasts of a leaf, chlorophyll catches light. The energy in that light is used to pull apart water molecules and join their hydrogen to carbon from *carbon dioxide*, a gas in the air. The result is a sugar called glucose. Leftover oxygen from the water is released into the air. In short: carbon dioxide plus water plus light makes sugar plus oxygen.

The sugar is both fuel and building material. Some of it the plant burns for energy. Some it links into long chains to make cellulose, the tough fiber in wood and cell walls. So the trunk of the oak is mostly carbon that was once floating in the air, captured one molecule at a time by leaves.

This is why leaves are flat and thin: to catch as much light as possible. It is why a plant on a windowsill bends toward the glass. And it is why nearly every food chain on Earth begins with a plant, an alga, or a photosynthetic bacterium. They are the only living things that can turn sunlight into the sugar every other organism needs.

words.d: the process in which plants use light energy to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water
a gas in the air that plants take in to build sugar; animals breathe it out as waste
a simple sugar that cells use as fuel

look.title: Only in the Light
look.text: In 1779 the Dutch doctor Jan Ingenhousz put leaves under water in glass jars and watched for bubbles. He reported that green leaves gave off the good air, the gas we now call oxygen, only when they were in sunlight, and that they stopped in the dark. Roots, flowers, and the non-green parts of plants did not give it off at all.
look.prompt: Ingenhousz found the bubbles came only from green parts and only in light. What two ingredients of photosynthesis does that point to?

check.q: Where does most of the material in a tree trunk come from?
check.why: The carbon in wood is captured from carbon dioxide in the air during photosynthesis.

check.q: What does a plant release into the air during photosynthesis?
check.why: Oxygen left over from splitting water is released. Sugar stays in the plant.

check.q: A plant is kept in total darkness for a week with plenty of water and soil. What happens?
choices: It makes sugar from the soil
It cannot make sugar and starts to weaken
It turns the water into oxygen
check.why: Without light there is no energy to build sugar, so the plant runs down its stored food.

lessons.title: Getting Energy Out of Food
lessons.mainIdea: Cellular respiration breaks sugar down with oxygen to release energy, the reverse of photosynthesis.
reading: The bee in the clover has a problem a plant does not. She cannot make sugar. She has to get it from flowers, and then she has to turn it into flight. Flight is expensive. A honeybee's wings beat about 200 times a second. The energy for that comes from breaking the sugar apart again, inside her mitochondria.

This breaking apart is *cellular respiration*. Sugar combines with oxygen and is taken apart step by step. Each step releases energy that the cell stores in a molecule called *ATP*, a kind of rechargeable battery. Carbon dioxide and water are left over. Written out, it is the mirror image of photosynthesis: sugar plus oxygen makes carbon dioxide plus water plus energy.

Every living thing does cellular respiration, including plants. A plant makes sugar in the daytime and burns some of it around the clock to power its own cells. The difference is that a plant makes more sugar than it burns, so it grows. An animal cannot make any, so it must eat.

You can feel respiration at work. Your body is warm because releasing energy also releases heat. You breathe out carbon dioxide because that is the waste. And when you sprint until your legs burn, you have hit the point where your muscle cells are using oxygen faster than your blood can deliver it.

words.d: the process in which cells break sugar down with oxygen to release energy
a small molecule that stores energy inside a cell and gives it up when the cell needs it

look.title: Two Equations, One Cycle
look.text: Write photosynthesis on the board: carbon dioxide + water + light energy → sugar + oxygen. Now write cellular respiration under it: sugar + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy for the cell. Cover the arrows and look only at the ingredients and products. Everything one process makes, the other one uses.
look.prompt: If plants and animals were sealed in a glass box with light, which gases would go around and around? What would be the only thing that has to keep coming in from outside?

check.q: What is the waste gas produced by cellular respiration?
check.why: Breaking sugar down with oxygen leaves carbon dioxide and water.

check.q: Which of these organisms carries out cellular respiration?
choices: Plants, animals, and bacteria all do
check.why: Every living cell needs energy, so every organism, including plants, does respiration.

check.q: Why is your body warm?
choices: Releasing energy from food also releases heat
The skin makes heat from sunlight
check.why: Cellular respiration in trillions of cells gives off heat as a side effect.

lessons.title: The Willow and the Mint
lessons.mainIdea: Careful experiments showed that plants build themselves from air and water, and that they restore the air animals use up.
reading: Around 1640 a Flemish doctor named Jan Baptist van Helmont wanted to know what a tree is made of. He dried 200 pounds of soil, put it in a pot, and planted a willow shoot that weighed 5 pounds. For five years he gave it only rainwater and kept dust off the pot. Then he pulled the tree up and weighed it: about 169 pounds. He dried the soil and weighed it again. It had lost only about 2 ounces.

Van Helmont concluded that the tree was made of water. He was half right. He had no way to know that the tree had also pulled carbon out of the air. But his method was the important thing. He measured before and after, controlled what went in, and let the numbers argue. The soil was not the source. Something else was.

A century later, in 1771, the English chemist Joseph Priestley sealed a burning candle in a jar. It went out, and a mouse placed in the same used-up air could not survive. Then he put a sprig of mint in the jar for some days. After that, a candle could burn again and a mouse could breathe. The plant had restored something to the air. Priestley did not yet know the gas was oxygen, and he did not know light was needed. Ingenhousz showed that part in 1779.

Put the three experiments together and you have the outline of a cycle. Plants take in water and carbon dioxide and give off oxygen. Animals take in oxygen and food and give off carbon dioxide. Matter goes around. Energy comes in from the sun, passes through, and leaves as heat. No single scientist saw the whole loop, but each measured one piece honestly.

words.d: a test set up so that one thing changes and everything else stays the same
the way atoms such as carbon move from air to plants to animals and back again

look.title: Van Helmont's Willow
look.cite: J. B. van Helmont, Ortus Medicinae, published 1648; rounded figures
look.prompt: The tree gained about 164 pounds and the soil lost about an eighth of a pound. What does that rule out, and what did van Helmont miss?

check.q: What did van Helmont's willow experiment rule out as the main source of a tree's mass?
check.why: The soil lost only about 2 ounces while the tree gained about 164 pounds, so soil was not the source.

check.q: What did Priestley's mint do to the used-up air in the jar?
choices: Restored the gas that candles and mice need
check.why: After the mint had been in the jar, a candle could burn and a mouse could breathe again.

check.q: Why do scientists praise van Helmont's method even though his conclusion was only half right?
choices: He measured carefully and let the numbers decide
He used the biggest tree he could find
He proved plants are made of soil
check.why: Weighing before and after, and controlling what went in, is the core of a fair experiment.

lessons.title: Sensory Receptors
lessons.mainIdea: Sensory receptors are cells that turn light, sound, chemicals, pressure, or heat into nerve signals.
reading: A bee finds a clover blossom from meters away. A hawk spots a mouse from high above. You smell toast from another room. None of this would happen without *sensory receptors*, special cells that detect one kind of thing in the world and turn it into a nerve signal. Every sense begins with a receptor.

Your eyes hold receptors that respond to light. Your ears hold tiny hair-like cells that bend when sound waves push on them. Your skin holds receptors for pressure, for heat and cold, and for damage, which you feel as pain. Your nose and tongue hold receptors that fit certain chemicals the way a lock fits a key. When a molecule from toast lands on the right receptor, that cell fires.

Each receptor sends the same kind of message: an electrical pulse along a nerve. What makes it a smell or a sound is not the pulse itself. It is where the pulse ends up in the brain. Signals from the eye go to the back of the brain, and the brain reads them as sight. That is why a hard bump on the back of the head can make you see stars.

Different animals have different receptors, so they live in different worlds. Bees see ultraviolet light that is invisible to you, and many flowers have ultraviolet patterns that point to nectar. Dogs have far more smell receptors than you. Some snakes have pits that sense the heat of a warm body in the dark. A sense is a window, and each species has its own set of windows.

words.d: cells that detect something in the world, such as light or sound, and turn it into a nerve signal
anything a receptor can detect, such as light, heat, sound, or a chemical
light with a wavelength shorter than violet, invisible to people but seen by bees

look.title: The Flower a Bee Sees
look.text: To your eye, a black-eyed Susan is a ring of plain yellow petals around a dark center. Photographed with a camera that records ultraviolet light, the same flower looks different: the outer petals are bright, but the inner half of each petal near the center is dark. The result looks like a target, a dark bull's-eye right where the nectar and pollen are.
look.prompt: Why might a flower with a hidden ultraviolet bull's-eye get more visits from bees than one without? Who benefits?

check.q: What does a sensory receptor do?
choices: Turns a stimulus such as light or sound into a nerve signal
check.why: Receptors are the cells at the start of every sense that convert a stimulus into an electrical pulse.

check.q: Why can a bee see a pattern on a flower that you cannot?
choices: Bees are closer to the flower
Bees have receptors for ultraviolet light and you do not
check.why: Bee eyes have receptors for ultraviolet, so patterns in that light are visible to them.

check.q: A signal from a receptor in your ear and a signal from your eye are both electrical pulses. What makes one a sound and the other a sight?
choices: The pulse from the ear is louder
The eye pulse is a different color
Where each signal ends up in the brain
check.why: All nerve signals are alike. The brain reads them by which region receives them.

lessons.title: Signals to the Brain
lessons.mainIdea: Nerve signals travel along neurons to the brain, which processes them and sends back commands.
reading: You step on a sharp pebble at the beach at Montrose Harbor. In about a tenth of a second, your foot lifts. In the moment after, you feel it. That tiny gap tells you something about how the *nervous system* works. Signals take time to travel, and the body is wired so that the most urgent ones take the shortest path.

A receptor in the skin fires and sends an electrical pulse along a *neuron*. Neurons are long. A single one can run from your toe to your spinal cord. At the end of the neuron, the pulse triggers the release of a chemical that crosses a tiny gap to the next neuron. That handoff is called a *synapse*. Signal, handoff, signal, handoff, all the way to the brain.

Nerve signals are fast, but not instant. The fastest fibers in your body, which carry touch and muscle signals, move at about 100 meters per second. Slow pain fibers crawl at about 1 meter per second. That is why a stubbed toe gives you a quick sharp jolt and then, a moment later, a dull ache. Two different fibers carried two different messages.

The brain does not just receive. It sorts, compares, and decides. Then it sends signals back down through motor neurons to muscles and organs. When you catch a ball, your eyes report its path, the brain predicts where it will be, and commands go to your arm before the ball arrives. All of it, sense to decision to action, takes less than half a second.

words.d: the brain, spinal cord, and nerves that carry signals and control the body
a nerve cell that carries electrical signals
the tiny gap between two neurons where a chemical passes the signal across

look.title: How Fast Signals Travel
rows: Fast touch and muscle nerve fiber
look.cite: standard physiology and physics reference values, rounded
look.prompt: A nerve signal has to go from a giraffe's hoof to its brain, about 4 meters, and back. Roughly how long would that take on the fast fibers? Why would slow fibers be a problem for a big animal?

check.q: What happens at a synapse?
choices: A chemical carries the signal across a gap to the next neuron
Blood delivers oxygen to the nerve
check.why: Neurons do not touch. A chemical released at the synapse passes the message across the gap.

check.q: Why do you feel a sharp jolt and then a dull ache when you stub your toe?
choices: The ache is from a second injury
Fast fibers carry the jolt and slow fibers carry the ache
The brain forgets and then remembers
The toe sends only one signal that echoes
check.why: Different nerve fibers carry signals at different speeds, so the messages arrive at different times.

check.q: When you catch a ball, in what order do things happen?
choices: Muscles move, then the brain decides, then the eyes see
The brain decides, then the eyes see, then muscles move
The eyes see, the brain decides, then muscles move
The ball is caught before any signal is sent
check.why: Sense, decide, act: receptors report, the brain predicts, motor neurons command the muscles.

lessons.title: Memory and Learning
lessons.mainIdea: Experiences change the connections between neurons, and those changes are memories that guide behavior.
reading: The honeybee from the story returns to the same patch of clover the next morning. She remembers where it is, and she remembers that it paid well. A memory is not a picture stored in a box. It is a change in the brain. When two neurons fire together often, the *synapse* between them gets stronger. The next time one fires, the other is more likely to follow. That strengthened path is a memory.

Around 1900, the Russian scientist Ivan Pavlov studied how dogs make saliva when they eat. He noticed something odd. The dogs began to drool when they heard the footsteps of the person who fed them, before any food appeared. So he tested it. He sounded a signal, such as a ticking metronome, and then gave food. After enough pairings, the sound alone made the dogs drool. The dogs had learned that one thing predicts another.

This kind of learning is everywhere. A bee learns which color of flower has nectar today. A squirrel in Lincoln Park learns which bench means a person with peanuts. You learn that a certain ringtone means a friend. All of it is the same rule: experiences that go together get linked in the brain.

Memory guides *behavior*, which is anything an organism does in response to its world. Some behavior is built in from birth, like a baby's grasp or a spider's web. Other behavior is learned. Most animals use a mix. The bee is born knowing how to fly and sting, but she has to learn where the clover is.

words.d: the connection between two neurons; it grows stronger when both fire together often
anything an organism does in response to its world, either built in or learned
a change in behavior that comes from experience

look.title: Pavlov's Dogs Drool at a Signal
look.text: Pavlov described a dog that had, many times, heard a metronome tick shortly before food was placed in its mouth. In his account, after those pairings the ticking sound alone caused the dog to produce saliva and turn toward the food dish, even though no food was present. He called this a conditioned reflex, to separate it from the built-in reflex of drooling at food itself.
look.cite: Ivan Pavlov, lectures on conditioned reflexes, based on experiments from about 1900 onward
look.prompt: Pavlov made a point of testing the sound alone, with no food. Why was that step necessary to prove the dogs had learned something?

check.q: What is a memory, in terms of the brain?
choices: A picture stored in one cell
A strengthened connection between neurons that fired together
check.why: Repeated firing strengthens synapses, and that changed path is the memory.

check.q: In Pavlov's experiment, what did the sound alone come to cause?
choices: The dogs barked at the food
check.why: After many pairings of sound and food, the sound by itself triggered saliva.

check.q: Which of these is a learned behavior?
choices: A bee remembering which patch of clover paid best
A spider spinning its first web
check.why: The bee's knowledge of a specific patch comes from experience. The others are built in.

lessons.title: Courtship and Display
lessons.mainIdea: Many animals use signals, songs, and dances to attract a mate, which increases their chances of having offspring.
reading: On a summer night in an Illinois field, hundreds of small lights blink on and off just above the grass. They are fireflies, and every flash is a message. A male flies and flashes a pattern. A female on a blade of grass answers with her own flash after a set pause. Each species has its own timing. Get it right and the male finds his mate. That is *courtship*: behavior whose purpose is to find and win a mate.

Courtship comes in many forms. Male peacocks spread a fan of eyed feathers and rattle it. Sandhill cranes, which pass through Illinois each spring, leap and bow in pairs. Frogs in a pond call all night, each species with a different croak. Male songbirds sing to claim a patch of territory and to show that they are healthy enough to sing for hours.

Why go to the trouble? Because reproduction only counts if it happens. An animal that never finds a mate leaves no offspring, and its traits end with it. An animal whose signal works leaves offspring that carry the signal. Over many generations, the signals that work best become common. A firefly's flash timing and a peacock's tail are the result.

Displays also carry information. A bright, long tail is costly to grow and hard to carry. A male that has one is showing that he found enough food and dodged enough predators to afford it. Choosing him is a way of choosing healthy genes for the young. Courtship is a conversation, and it is one of the main reasons animals look and act the way they do.

words.d: behavior an animal uses to attract and win a mate, such as a song, dance, or display
the process by which living things make new living things of their own kind
the young of an organism

look.title: Flash Codes in the Grass
look.text: You lie on your back in the grass at dusk and watch. One kind of firefly gives a single long flash while swooping upward, drawing a J shape in the air. Another gives a quick double flash. A third does a rapid flicker. Down in the grass, faint answering flashes come after a pause. When you shine a flashlight in a short pattern, a male drifts closer to investigate.
look.prompt: Why would it matter for each species to have its own flash pattern? What would happen if they all flashed the same way?

check.q: What is courtship?
choices: A way to hide from predators
Behavior used to attract and win a mate
check.why: Courtship behaviors, from songs to flashes, exist to find and win a mate.

check.q: A firefly species has a flash pattern that females rarely answer. What will happen to that pattern over many generations?
choices: It will spread to other species
It will stay exactly as common
It will become rare because those males leave few offspring
check.why: Traits that do not lead to offspring are not passed on and fade out of the population.

check.q: What might a peacock's large, bright tail tell a female?
choices: He has found enough food and stayed healthy enough to afford it
check.why: A costly display is a signal of health, which suggests healthy genes for the offspring.

lessons.title: Flowers and Pollinators
lessons.mainIdea: Flowers are structures that attract animals to carry pollen, and their shapes match the animals that visit them.
reading: A plant cannot walk to find a mate. So flowering plants hire couriers. A *flower* is a structure built to get *pollen*, which carries the male half of a seed, from one plant to another. Some plants let the wind do it and make huge clouds of tiny pollen, which is why grasses and ragweed make people sneeze. Others make a flower that pays an animal to carry it.

A flower advertises with color and scent, and it pays in nectar or extra pollen. Bees, butterflies, moths, hummingbirds, beetles, and even some bats are *pollinators*. When one pushes into a flower for the reward, pollen sticks to it. At the next flower of the same kind, some rubs off onto a sticky tip called the stigma. Pollen grains then grow down to the eggs inside, and seeds begin.

Flowers and their pollinators often match like a key and a lock. Hummingbird flowers are usually red, tube-shaped, and scentless, because hummingbirds see red well and have a poor sense of smell. Moth flowers are often white and open at night with a strong scent. Bee flowers are often blue or yellow with a landing platform and ultraviolet patterns.

Some flowers and their pollinators fit each other closely. A hummingbird's long bill reaches nectar deep inside a trumpet-shaped flower that most bees cannot reach. Night-blooming flowers are often white and strongly scented, which helps moths find them in the dark. The shape and color of a flower tell you a lot about who visits it.

words.d: the part of a plant that makes pollen and eggs and attracts animals to carry the pollen
tiny grains from a flower that carry the male half of what is needed to make a seed
animals such as bees and hummingbirds that carry pollen from flower to flower

look.title: Match the Flower
look.text: Flower A is red and shaped like a long tube, with no smell. Flower B is flat and yellow, with a landing platform and a sweet smell. Flower C is white, opens at night and smells strong.
look.prompt: Match each flower to its likely visitor: a moth, a bee or a hummingbird. Give one clue for each choice.

check.q: What is the job of a flower?
choices: To get pollen from one plant to another so seeds can form
check.why: Flowers make pollen and eggs and attract the animals that carry the pollen.

check.q: A flower is red, shaped like a tube, and has no scent. Which pollinator is it most likely built for?
check.why: Hummingbirds see red well, have a poor sense of smell, and feed from tubes with their long beaks.

check.q: Why do grasses and ragweed make so much pollen?
choices: Because they have very large flowers
Because bees eat most of it
Because they rely on the wind, which wastes most of the pollen
check.why: Wind carries pollen at random, so wind-pollinated plants make huge amounts to ensure some lands on another plant.

lessons.title: Seeds on the Move
lessons.mainIdea: Plants have structures that move seeds away from the parent so the young plants are not crowded out.
reading: Drop a maple seed and watch it. It does not fall. It spins like a tiny helicopter and drifts sideways on the breeze. That spin is not an accident. A seed that lands under its own parent grows in the parent's shade and competes with it for water. A seed that lands farther away has a better chance. Moving seeds away is called *seed dispersal*, and plants have many tools for it.

Some seeds ride the wind. Maples have wings. Dandelions and milkweed have fluffy parachutes. Some seeds ride water. A coconut can float across an ocean and sprout on a new beach. Some seeds explode. Touch a ripe jewelweed pod along an Illinois creek and it bursts, flinging seeds a meter or more.

Many seeds ride animals. Burrs have hooks that grab fur and socks. In the 1940s a Swiss engineer pulled burrs off his dog, looked at the hooks under a microscope, and invented the hook-and-loop fastener we now call Velcro. Other seeds hide inside fruit. A bird eats a berry, flies off, and drops the seed later, packaged in fertilizer. Squirrels bury acorns and forget some, which is how many oaks get planted.

A fruit, then, is a plant's way of paying an animal to move its seeds, just as nectar pays a bee to move pollen. Sweet, bright fruit says: eat me, carry me. The plant loses some sugar and gains a courier. Once again, two very different living things end up working together, without either one intending it.

words.d: the movement of seeds away from the parent plant by wind, water, animals, or bursting
the part of a plant that holds seeds; many are sweet so animals will eat them and carry the seeds

look.title: A Handful of Seeds
look.text: Spread five seeds on a table: a maple seed with a papery wing, a dandelion seed with a fluffy tuft, a burr covered in tiny hooks, a smooth acorn, and a cherry pit with a bit of sweet flesh still on it. Each one is built to travel a different way. Blow on them, drop them, brush a wool sleeve over them, and see which move.
look.prompt: Match each seed to how it travels. Which of these would you expect to land closest to the parent, and which farthest?

check.q: Why is it useful for seeds to land away from the parent plant?
choices: They avoid competing with the parent for light and water
Seeds cannot sprout in shade at all
check.why: A seed under the parent is shaded and shares the same soil, so it is less likely to thrive.

check.q: A seed has a papery wing that makes it spin as it falls. How does it travel?
check.why: Wings and parachutes catch the wind and carry the seed sideways.

check.q: Why do many plants surround their seeds with sweet fruit?
choices: So animals will eat the fruit and carry the seed away
check.why: Fruit is a payment. The animal gets sugar and the seed gets a free ride and some fertilizer.

lessons.title: Caring for the Young
lessons.mainIdea: Some animals make many offspring and give little care; others make few and protect them, and both strategies can work.
reading: A female salmon lays thousands of eggs in a gravel riverbed and then dies. She never sees a single one hatch. An emperor penguin lays one egg, and the father balances it on his feet under a fold of skin through two months of Antarctic winter, without eating. Both are ways of making sure there is a next generation. They are just very different bets.

The salmon's bet is numbers. Most of her eggs will be eaten. But if even two of thousands survive to adulthood, she has replaced herself and her mate. The penguin's bet is care. One egg is precious, so the parents guard it, warm it, and feed the chick for months. Fewer young, but each one has a much better chance.

Many animals fall between. A robin in a Chicago backyard lays about four eggs, sits on them for two weeks, and then feeds the chicks until they can fly. An alligator guards her nest and carries hatchlings to water in her mouth. Wolves and elephants raise young in groups, where aunts and older siblings help. Humans give more care, for longer, than almost any other animal.

Plants make the same kind of bet. A dandelion scatters hundreds of tiny seeds and provides each with almost nothing. A coconut palm makes a few enormous seeds, each packed with food and water for the seedling. Whether the strategy is many-and-cheap or few-and-costly, the goal is the same: enough offspring survive to carry on.

words.d: anything a parent does to protect, feed, or teach its young
a pattern of behavior that helps an organism survive or reproduce, shaped over many generations

look.title: Two Nests on the Same River
look.text: On a bank of a river in Illinois, a snapping turtle digs a hole, lays about 30 eggs, covers them with dirt, and walks back to the water. She will never return. In a tree above, a pair of bald eagles tends two eggs in a nest they have used for years, taking turns keeping them warm and bringing fish to the chicks for nearly three months after hatching.
look.prompt: Which nest do you expect to have more survivors per egg? Why might both strategies still keep their species going?

check.q: Why can a salmon leave thousands of eggs with no care and still succeed?
choices: The river takes care of them
Even if only a few survive, that is enough to replace the parents
check.why: Making many offspring is a numbers game. A few survivors out of thousands keeps the population going.

check.q: Which animal in the lesson gives the most care to a single egg?
check.why: The penguin father guards one egg on his feet through the Antarctic winter.

check.q: How is a coconut like an emperor penguin egg?
choices: Both are few in number and given a lot of resources
Both are made by the thousands
check.why: Both are the few-and-costly strategy: a small number of offspring, each well supplied.

lessons.title: Genes and Environment
lessons.mainIdea: How an organism grows depends on both the genes it inherits and the conditions it lives in.
reading: Plant two seeds from the same sunflower. Put one in rich soil by a sunny window and the other in a dark closet with little water. In a month, one is tall and green and the other is pale and thin. They started with the same instructions. What differed was the *environment*. Growth is never just genes or just surroundings. It is always both.

Genes set the range. A sunflower seed will never grow into an oak, no matter how well you treat it. A person's genes shape their eye color, their basic body plan, and roughly how tall they can grow. That information came from their parents and is written in the DNA of every cell.

The environment decides where in the range the organism ends up. For a plant, that means light, water, nutrients in the soil, and temperature. For an animal, it means food, disease, stress, and exercise. Children who get enough food and avoid serious illness grow closer to the top of the range their genes allow. Identical twins share the same genes, but if one plays a sport and the other does not, their bodies will differ.

This is why a question like 'Is it genes or environment?' usually has the same answer: yes. The two are not rivals. Genes are a recipe, and the environment is the kitchen. The same recipe can come out very differently depending on what is in the kitchen.

words.d: the instructions, written in DNA and passed from parents, that shape how an organism grows
everything around an organism that can affect it: light, water, food, temperature, other living things
a feature of an organism, such as height or leaf shape

look.title: Same Seeds, Two Windows
look.text: A teacher plants twelve bean seeds from one packet in twelve identical cups of the same soil. Six cups go on a south-facing windowsill and get water every day. Six go on a shelf in the corner and get water every other day. After three weeks, the windowsill beans average 25 centimeters tall with dark green leaves. The corner beans average 12 centimeters, and they are pale and leaning toward the door.
look.prompt: What did the two groups share, and what was different? Which of the differences in the results are caused by the environment, and how do you know?

check.q: Two plants from the same seed packet grow to very different heights. What most likely explains it?
choices: Height is not affected by anything
check.why: Seeds from one packet share nearly the same genes, so the difference must come from conditions.

check.q: Which of these is set mainly by genes?
choices: How much a plant is watered
Whether a child gets enough food
Whether a seed grows into a sunflower or an oak
check.why: The kind of organism is written in its DNA. The other choices are environmental.

check.q: Identical twins have the same genes. What is the best reason their bodies could still differ?
check.why: The environment, including food, exercise, and illness, shapes how the same genes play out.

lessons.title: Testing What Helps Growth
lessons.mainIdea: A fair test changes one factor at a time and compares against a control to find out what really affects growth.
reading: Suppose you want to know whether a certain fertilizer makes radishes grow faster. You could add it to a pot and see what happens. But if the radishes grow well, was it the fertilizer, the sunny week, or the good seeds? To find out, you need a *fair test*, an experiment set up so that only one thing changes.

Start with two groups of plants that are as alike as possible: same seeds, same soil, same pots, same window, same water. Give one group the fertilizer and the other none. The group without is the *control*. It shows what happens on its own. The one factor you change, the fertilizer, is the *variable*. Everything else is held the same so it cannot hide the answer.

Then measure, do not just look. Count leaves, measure height in centimeters, weigh the radishes at the end. Use several plants in each group, because any one plant might be odd. Van Helmont used one willow. A modern scientist would use many, and would compare the average of each group.

If the fertilized group grows clearly taller than the control, you have evidence the fertilizer helped. If both groups grow the same, you have learned something too. And if one fertilized plant died, that is a reason to look again, not a reason to hide it. A fair test is a way of asking nature a question so that you can trust the answer.

words.d: an experiment in which only one factor is changed and everything else is kept the same
the group in an experiment that does not get the change, used for comparison
the one factor that is deliberately changed in a fair test

look.title: A Test With a Flaw
look.text: A student wants to know if music helps plants grow. He puts one plant next to a speaker on a sunny windowsill and plays music every day. He puts a second plant in a quiet hallway with no windows. After two weeks the plant by the speaker is much taller. He writes: music helps plants grow.
look.prompt: What is wrong with this test? Which factors changed besides the music, and how would you fix the setup so the result could be trusted?

check.q: What is the purpose of a control group?
choices: To show what happens when nothing is changed, for comparison
To make sure every plant dies
check.why: Without a control you cannot tell whether the change you made caused the result.

check.q: In a test of whether fertilizer helps radishes, which should be the only difference between the groups?
check.why: The fertilizer is the variable. Light, seeds, and pots must be the same in both groups.

check.q: Why use several plants in each group instead of one?
choices: Because one plant uses too much water
Because any single plant might be unusual, and an average is more reliable
check.why: Averaging over many plants smooths out odd cases and makes the result trustworthy.

review.q: What does a plant need to make sugar by photosynthesis?
review.why: Light provides the energy, and water and carbon dioxide provide the atoms for glucose.

review.q: How are photosynthesis and cellular respiration related?
choices: Each one uses what the other one makes
review.why: Photosynthesis makes sugar and oxygen; respiration uses them and returns carbon dioxide and water.

review.q: Van Helmont's willow gained about 164 pounds while the soil lost about 2 ounces. What was the main source of the new mass?
choices: Water and carbon dioxide from the air
review.why: The soil barely changed, so the tree's material came from water and, as later shown, carbon dioxide.

review.q: Which part of the body turns a stimulus such as light into a nerve signal?
review.why: Receptors are the cells at the start of every sense that convert a stimulus into a signal.

review.q: In Pavlov's experiment, why did the dogs drool at the sound alone?
choices: They had learned that the sound predicted food
review.why: Repeated pairing linked the sound and the food in the dogs' brains, a learned behavior.

review.q: A flower is white, opens at night, and has a strong sweet scent. Which pollinator is it most likely built for?
review.why: Moths fly at night and find flowers by scent, so pale, fragrant night flowers suit them.

review.q: Which is an example of seed dispersal by animals?
choices: A maple seed spinning in the wind
A coconut floating on the sea
A bird eating a berry and dropping the seed far away
review.why: Fruit pays the bird to carry the seed. The other three use wind, water, and bursting.

review.q: Two bean plants with the same genes grow to different heights. What is the most likely cause?
review.why: With the same genes, differences in light, water, and nutrients explain the different growth.
